1. Introduction

1.1 This Explanatory Memorandum has been prepared by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and is laid before Parliament by Command of His Majesty.

1.2 This Explanatory Memorandum contains information for the Secondary Legislation Scrutiny Committee.

2. Declaration

2.1 Florence Eshalomi MP, Minister of State for Homelessness, Democracy, Communities and Faith, confirms that this Explanatory Memorandum meets the required standard.

2.2 Jonathan Eddy, Deputy Director for Communities Governance and Institutions, confirms that this Explanatory Memorandum meets the required standard.

3. Contact

3.1 Specific and technical written queries from Parliament relating to the Private Parking Code of Practice should be directed to Jaspreet Bains at parking@communities.gov.uk. General queries and correspondence related to private parking can also be directed to the Off-Street Parking Policy team at this inbox.

Part One: Explanation and context

4. Overview of the Instrument

What does the legislation do?

4.1 The Parking (Code of Practice) Act 2019 (‘the Act’) places a duty on the Secretary of State to prepare a Code of Practice (‘the Code’) containing guidance about the operation and management of private parking facilities. The Act originated as a Private Members’ Bill, reflecting longstanding cross-party concern about poor practice in the private parking sector and the need for consistent national standards.

4.2 The Code must contain guidance that promotes good practice in the operation and management of private parking facilities, and guidance about appeals against parking charges.

4.3 While the Code itself is not directly enforceable in law, the Act provides mechanisms to secure compliance, including powers to restrict access to Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (‘DVLA’) vehicle keeper data for operators that fail to adhere to the Code’s requirements.

Where does the legislation extend to and apply?

4.4 The Code extends and applies to England and Wales and Scotland.

5. Policy Context

What is being done and why?

5.1 The government is introducing a Code in compliance with its duties arising from the Act, as set out in section 4 of this Explanatory Memorandum.

5.2 Since the introduction of the Act, there have been improvements in how the private parking industry operates. Despite this, concerns continue to be raised about the prevalence of poor practice. The government’s Call for Evidence, published in July 2023, and the subsequent consultation, published in July 2025, demonstrated ongoing concerns among motorists about standards across the sector[footnote 1]. A government Code is therefore needed to achieve the aims of the Act: to raise standards across the private parking industry and protect motorists from poor practice. It is also a legal requirement because the Act places a duty on the Secretary of State to prepare this Code.

5.3 The Code will establish clear, consistent rules for operators and motorists, reduce unfair charges being issued and pursued, build trust through predictable appeal outcomes, and drive compliant operator behaviour across parking sites whilst holding non-compliant operators to account.

5.4 The Code introduces a range of new protections, including:

minimum, mandatory, 5-minute consideration periods before a driver is deemed to have parked (except pre-booked parking)

a mandatory, 10-minute grace period before enforcement action can be taken (except short stay car parks)

stronger requirements for appeals handling

a defined list of circumstances where parking charges must be cancelled on appeal or charges reduced to £20 through the Appeals Charter

protections for disabled motorists and other vulnerable groups; and

stronger governance and compliance arrangements

5.5 The approach seeks to balance the interests of motorists with the legitimate need for landowners and operators to manage parking on private land effectively.

5.6 The Code is supported by a compliance framework under which access to DVLA vehicle keeper data will be linked to compliance with the Code. Compliance will be assessed through an independently assured Certification Scheme recognised by the United Kingdom Accreditation Service.

What was the previous policy, how is this different?

5.7 The parking industry is currently regulated through a Sector Single Code (‘Sector Code’), published by the parking trade associations in June 2024 and brought into effect in October 2024. It represented a significant industry-led step to raise standards after 2019.

5.8 The Sector Code is largely based on the previous government’s Code of Practice, which was laid before Parliament in February 2022 before being withdrawn in June 2022. The Sector Code adopted a number of principles from the withdrawn Code, including a single set of standards for operators, a 28-day appeals period, and specific requirements relating to signage. However, important differences remained, including the length of consideration and grace periods, the introduction of a £20 reduced charge, and the circumstances in which appeals could be made after a parking charge had been paid.

5.9 Furthermore, the responses to government’s Call for Evidence in 2023 and consultation in 2025 showed concerns remained about poor practice and the effectiveness of compliance monitoring. The absence of independent oversight, coupled with differences in auditing approaches and limited transparency around enforcement activity, undermined confidence that standards were being applied consistently across the sector.

5.10 The government’s new Code as detailed in section 4 will replace the existing Sector Code when it comes into force.

6. Legislative and Legal Context

Impact on businesses, charities and voluntary bodies

9.3 The impact on business, charities or voluntary bodies is considered proportionate by government. Compliance with the Code will require members of the private parking sector to make changes to their practices due to the strengthened protections for motorists. There will also be enhanced data collection requirements directing parking operators and accredited parking associations to disclose relevant data to the government. While there will be compliance costs, the Impact Assessment concludes that a single government Code will provide greater clarity, consistency and certainty across the sector.

9.4 The legislation may affect small or micro businesses. Evidence provided to the government shows that the vast majority of parking operators are small or medium-sized businesses. Using an illustrative scenario involving a 5% reduction in the number of parking charge notices issued, the government estimates a £320 million reduction in parking charge revenue, partly offset by £2.3 million in savings from fewer second-stage appeals.

9.5 However, providing an exemption for these businesses would exclude a significant number of operators, which risks creating an uneven environment in which motorists receive different levels of protection depending on which company manages a particular site. This would weaken the effectiveness of the Code and prevent it from providing greater consistency and improved standards across the entire sector. Parking charges may in the absence of this Code provide a revenue stream for operators but their primary purpose, as set out by operators in response to our consultation in 2025, is to discourage motorists from breaking the rules and to protect the revenue raised through parking tariffs.

9.6 The impact on the public sector is related primarily to the compliance and administration of the new framework, with the total cost assessed at £0.69 million. This includes monitoring compliance and performance data, supporting the Scrutiny and Oversight Board, and undertaking periodic reviews of the Code. These costs have been assessed in the accompanying Impact Assessment and are expected to be outweighed by the benefits of improved standards, transparency and consistency across the private parking sector.

10. Monitoring and review

What is the approach to monitoring and reviewing this legislation?

10.1 The Code will be kept under review in accordance with section 3 of the Act. Any future revisions will be subject to the consultation requirements set out in section 2 of the Act.

10.2 A Scrutiny and Oversight Board will be established to review data and evidence relating to the operation of the Code and provide recommendations to government on potential future changes.

Part Three: Statements and Matters of Particular Interest to Parliament

11. Matters of Special Interest to Parliament

Parliamentary Scrutiny

11.1 This Code fulfils the government’s statutory duty under the Act to prepare a Code containing guidance about the operation and management of private parking facilities.

On 20 October 2026, this Code was laid before Parliament. The Code will now be subject to a 40-day period of Parliamentary scrutiny before it can be issued.

The Code will come into force 21 calendar days from the point of issue.

The transitional enforcement arrangements for new standards will be published on GOV.UK when the Code comes into force.

12. European Convention on Human Rights

12.1 As the instrument is subject to negative resolution procedure and does not amend primary legislation, no statement is required.

13. The Relevant European Union Acts

13.1 This instrument is not made under the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018, the European Union (Future Relationship) Act 2020 or the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 (“relevant European Union Acts”).

Both the Consultation and Response can be viewed here: Private Parking Code of Practice. ↩
